analysis.one_liner: Lets companies share customer internet data with the government, with legal immunity and no public disclosure.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 288-127 on April 18, 2013, but the Senate never voted, and the bill died when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: CISPA would let companies monitor their own networks and share customers' communications and personal data with federal agencies to defend against cyberattacks. Companies that shared data in good faith would be shielded from lawsuits, and anything shared with the government would be exempt from the Freedom of Information Act and from state public-records laws. In return, cleared companies could receive classified threat intelligence directly from agencies like the NSA.
analysis.who_benefits: Large internet, telecom, and cybersecurity companies gain the most: immunity from civil and criminal suits for monitoring networks and sharing user data, exemption of shared information from FOIA and state disclosure laws, a bar on regulators using the shared data, and preemption of state privacy statutes. Cleared companies would also get classified cyber threat intelligence and expedited security clearances for their staff. Intelligence and law-enforcement agencies would gain real-time feeds of private-network threat data, usable for cybersecurity crimes and for crimes involving serious bodily harm or offenses against minors. The public benefit claimed by supporters is faster government-industry coordination that makes banking, utilities, and other services harder to hack.

how_it_helps.text: Companies would gain broad legal immunity to monitor their own networks and share customers' data with the government, removing the threat of lawsuits under existing privacy laws.
Information shared with the government would be exempt from the Freedom of Information Act and state public-records laws, and could not be used by the government for regulatory purposes.

Certified companies could receive classified cyber threat intelligence directly from intelligence agencies, with the Director of National Intelligence authorized to grant expedited security clearances to company employees and contractors.

Supporters argued that real-time sharing of threat data between the government and private networks would help prevent, respond to, and recover from cyberattacks on utilities, banks, and other services the public depends on.

analysis.who_pays: Internet users and customers pay in privacy: companies could monitor their communications and hand personal data to the government without liability, the public could not find out what was shared through FOIA or state public-records requests, and state laws restricting these activities would be overridden. If the government misused shared data, the only remedy would be a federal claim against the United States for intentional or willful violations, capped at actual damages or $1,000.
analysis.who_pays_short: Internet users, whose data could be shared

drawbacks.text: Companies could share Americans' personal communications and data with the government without facing lawsuits, and the public could never learn what was shared, since the information is exempt from the Freedom of Information Act and state disclosure laws.
The bill would supersede any state statute restricting these activities, overriding stronger state privacy protections.

Government use would not be limited to stopping hacks: shared information could also be used to investigate and prosecute crimes involving serious bodily harm and crimes against minors, a much broader set of purposes than cybersecurity.

Accountability for misuse is thin: only the government (not companies) can be sued, only for intentional or willful violations, for actual damages or $1,000, and that claim would be the exclusive remedy.
The House rejected, 189-224, a motion to recommit that would have added protections barring employers or the government from demanding workers' email and social media passwords without a court order.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Faster threat sharing has a real security payoff, and the bill does include minimization procedures, an affirmative-search restriction, and bans on using library, medical, tax, firearms, and education records. But the design tilts heavily toward the companies and agencies: immunity is sweeping, the secrecy exemptions are broad, the privacy rules would be written largely by the same security agencies doing the sharing, and the bill preempts state privacy laws. Even the Obama administration, which supported information sharing in principle, said this version lacked adequate privacy protections and threatened a veto (widely reported). A narrower bill with judicially enforceable limits could have captured much of the security benefit at far less privacy cost.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by a wide bipartisan margin, but the Senate committee it was sent to never acted, and the bill expired when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: The House Intelligence Committee, chaired by sponsor Mike Rogers, reported the bill on April 15, 2013, under a rule allowing one hour of debate and specified amendments.

Before final passage, House Democrats offered a motion to recommit that would have barred employers or the government from requiring workers' email and social media passwords without a court order; it failed 189-224, with 188 of 201 Democrats in favor and 1 of 231 Republicans.
The House passed the bill on April 18, 2013, 288-127, with 196 of 231 Republicans and 92 of 201 Democrats voting yes.
The Senate received the bill on April 22, 2013, and referred it to the Select Committee on Intelligence; the record shows no further action, and it died when the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Internet users and privacy advocates came out ahead: the sweeping corporate immunity, FOIA exemption, and state-law preemption never became law, and companies and intelligence agencies had to operate under the pre-existing, more limited sharing arrangements.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Internet users; the immunity never became law

for.name: Rep. Mike Rogers
for.role: Chairman, House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, reported it out of his committee on April 15, 2013, managed the floor debate, and offered amendments during consideration.

for.name: 92 of 201 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final passage, supplying more than a third of the winning total.

for.name: Major business and tech lobbies, including the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and firms such as IBM, AT&T, Verizon, and Intel
for.what_they_did: Lobbied for a liability shield and a legal channel to share threat data with the government; helped defeat an earlier version's backlash and pushed the 2013 reintroduction.

against.name: 98 of 201 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, providing nearly all of the 127 no votes; 188 of them also backed the failed privacy motion to recommit.

against.name: Rep. Ed Perlmutter
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit with instructions to add password-privacy and internet-firewall protections; the motion failed 189-224.

against.name: Obama administration
against.what_they_did: Repeatedly threatened to veto the bill over inadequate privacy and civil-liberties protections, weakening momentum in the Senate.

against.name: Privacy and civil liberties groups, including the Electronic Frontier Foundation, the ACLU, and the Center for Democracy and Technology
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the bill's liability immunity, FOIA exemption, and broad government use of shared data, generating large public petitions against it.

against.name: Senate Select Committee on Intelligence
against.role: Senate committee (chaired by Sen. Dianne Feinstein, D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on April 22, 2013, and took no further action on it; the chair preferred her own, more privacy-protective information-sharing approach.

sides.party_line_note: Passage was bipartisan on paper — 196 of 231 Republicans and 92 of 201 Democrats voted yes — but 98 of the 127 no votes came from Democrats, and the same day a Democratic privacy amendment failed 189-224 with just 1 Republican in favor.

industries.note: The bill gives these companies a free legal channel to monitor user communications and hand personal data to the government, plus immunity from suits and FOIA/state-disclosure exemptions that keep the sharing secret. Their gain — legal cover for data sharing — comes directly at the privacy cost their customers bear.

As 'cybersecurity providers,' they gain the right to monitor client networks and share threat data with immunity, and cleared firms would receive classified intelligence — expanding their market and government ties. Their core service of blocking attacks genuinely protects customers, but the immunity applies to the monitoring and data-sharing side, not just the defense.

industries.industry: Intelligence agencies and federal law enforcement (NSA, DHS, DOJ)
industries.note: Agencies would receive near-real-time threat data from private networks and could use it for cybersecurity crimes and any crime involving serious bodily harm or offenses against minors. The bill states it adds no surveillance authority, but it broadens the data pipeline and exempts it from public disclosure.
State statutes restricting the authorized activities would be superseded, and shared information exempted from state public-records laws, voiding stronger state privacy protections.
